name: Crypto Threat Is Overstated
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: No, Shor's Algorithm Is Not Coming for Your Password This Year
lesson.summary: Real long-term cryptographic risk gets separated from marketing urgency by comparing the actual qubit counts needed to break RSA against what quantum hardware can do today.
lesson.body:
Headlines routinely announce that quantum computers "will break all encryption," often with an implied sense that this is imminent. It is worth separating the physics claim, which has real substance, from the marketing claim, which mostly does not. The previous chapter's migration argument depends on taking the threat seriously over a multi-decade horizon; this chapter is about resisting the temptation to compress that horizon into next quarter's sales pitch.

Start with the number that matters most: how many qubits does breaking RSA-2048 actually take. A widely cited 2019 estimate by Gidney and Ekera put the requirement at roughly 20 million noisy physical qubits running for about eight days, using a surface-code error-correction scheme. Later refinements to algorithms and error-correction methods have lowered that figure somewhat, but credible estimates still sit in the range of one million to tens of millions of physical qubits, not thousands. These are theoretical projections that depend on assumptions about gate error rates and code distance, and serious researchers disagree by roughly an order of magnitude, so treat any single figure as illustrative rather than exact.

Now compare that to fielded hardware. As of the mid-2020s, the largest gate-based superconducting quantum processors hold on the order of a few hundred to roughly one thousand physical qubits, IBM's Condor chip, unveiled in 2023 with 1,121 qubits, is a representative example of the current ceiling. None of these machines runs meaningfully error-corrected logical qubits at any scale close to what breaking RSA-2048 would require. The distance between "about a thousand noisy physical qubits" and "a million-plus fault-tolerant logical qubits" is not a gap one more funding round closes; it likely spans several additional engineering breakthroughs in qubit quality, error-correction codes, control electronics, and cryogenic scaling, each of which has historically taken years.

This is exactly where the migration argument from the previous chapter does its real work. Because no one can rule out a cryptographically relevant quantum computer arriving within ten to fifteen years, and because migration realistically takes most of a decade on its own, prudent risk management still says start migrating now, even while telling colleagues honestly that nobody is decrypting this quarter's transactions. The overstatement in most quantum-threat marketing is not that the risk is fake, it is that a probabilistic, decades-long risk gets collapsed into artificial next-quarter urgency to close a sale.

The skeptic's discipline is to hold both ends of the timeline honestly. Do not say "never": the qubit-count gap has closed by roughly an order of magnitude in under a decade of hardware and algorithmic progress, and further surprises are plausible. Do not say "any day now" either: no credible public roadmap gets any lab from today's noisy few-hundred-qubit machines to millions of fault-tolerant qubits within just a few years. Treat this as a long-tailed risk to insure against methodically through migration, not a five-alarm fire that justifies buying whatever a vendor is selling this week.
